sections.h2: What is Towns County, Georgia like for homeowners?
sections.html:
Towns County is a small mountain county on the North Carolina line, with Hiawassee as the seat and Young Harris as the largest city. The state created it in 1856 and named it for a former governor, George W. Towns, per Wikipedia.

It covers 172 square miles in the Blue Ridge, and the Chattahoochee National Forest and a stretch of the Appalachian Trail lie partly inside it. Brasstown Bald, the highest peak in Georgia, rises in the southwest corner and straddles the Union County line. Lake Chatuge, created by the Tennessee Valley Authority's dam in 1942, fills the northeast and is the state's highest major lake. Cities are Hiawassee and Young Harris, and Tate City is a census-designated place.

The county's public schools share one campus east of Hiawassee, with an elementary, middle and high school under the Towns County School District. Young Harris College, founded in 1886, is also in the county. Tourism, the lake and outdoor recreation supply much of the work, and Wikipedia cites about 25 percent of jobs tied to recreation.

sections.h2: How do Towns County housing numbers differ from nearby counties?
sections.html:
Towns County stands out for older residents, higher home values and a very high owner-occupied share. QuickFacts shows 82.3% owner-occupied housing for 2020-2024 and a median home value of $316,100.

The county gained 6.4% in population from the 2020 base, the fastest growth of the four counties in this group. Households average 2.03 people, and the median age in the 2020 census was 57.2. That census counted 8,600 housing units, of which 36.4% were vacant, and a rental vacancy rate of 15.9%. Many of those empty units are seasonal or second homes, so a seller may be dealing with an owner who lives far away. Someone inheriting such a house or cabin needs the tax bill forwarded to a current address.

sections.h2: Who do you contact about property tax in Towns County?
sections.html:
The tax commissioner bills and collects at 48 River Street, Suite H, Hiawassee, GA 30546, inside the courthouse annex. The phone is (706) 896-2267, and hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, with the office closed for lunch from noon to 1 p.m. per the county government page.

The tax assessor is in Suite G at the same address, at (706) 896-3984, and keeps the same weekday hours. Parcel records are on qPublic, which the county says is a free service. Property tax can be paid online through the county tax site.

  • Tax commissioner: bills, payments, levies, mobile home tax
  • Tax assessor: valuations, returns, homestead and conservation applications, mobile home registration
  • Clerk of Superior Court: deeds, with copies available in the deed room

The county Board of Commissioners and the Board of Education set the millage rates each year. The tax commissioner does not.

sections.h2: When is Towns County property tax due, and why is it in January?
sections.html:
Real estate tax is due January 10, which is later than in most Georgia counties. The county's information page and its FAQ both give that date, and mailed payments must carry a United States Postal Service postmark, not a metered one.

After the due date, interest is added on the 10th of each month at prime plus 3%, divided by 12. A 5% penalty is added after 120 days and again every 120 days after that, up to a 20% cap. Bills for mobile homes are usually mailed on January 2, and tax is due April 1, with a 10% penalty added April 2.

  • Real estate: due January 10
  • Interest: monthly on the 10th, prime plus 3% divided by 12
  • Penalty: 5% at 120 days, repeating to a 20% maximum
  • Mobile homes: due April 1, 10% penalty on April 2

An account still unpaid after 12 months goes to a collection agency, and administration and levy fees of up to $215 and more can be added, along with newspaper advertising for four weeks before a sale. Pay or arrange terms before that stage.

sections.h2: What should a Towns County seller know about deferral and conservation use?
sections.html:
Two programs can follow a property into a sale. The first is the property tax deferral for homeowners 62 and older with gross household income of $15,000 or less. It lets them defer, not erase, the tax, and the county says deferred tax generally comes due when ownership changes or when it reaches 85% of fair market value.

The second is conservation use, which values qualifying farm or timber land at current use rather than market value. It requires a 10-year covenant with the Board of Tax Assessors. The assessor's page says a buyer who keeps the same use and signs the covenant avoids a penalty, while a change of use triggers penalties. Land in the mountains often carries such a covenant, so check the parcel before you list.

Ask the assessor's office at (706) 896-3984 whether either program applies to your parcel, and get the payoff or covenant terms in writing. A cash buyer who purchases as-is will still want those numbers before closing.

sections.h2: How do homestead exemptions work in Towns County?
sections.html:
The county tax site says the application goes to the Towns County Tax Assessor's Office, and first-time homeowners should bring a copy of the warranty deed. The deadline is April 1, and an application received after it applies to the next year.

You must own and occupy the home as of January 1. Once granted, the exemption renews each year, but a new application is needed after a move, a change of ownership, or a request for a different kind of exemption. The county says Towns County has local exemptions that replace the state amounts when the local amount is larger, so ask the assessor for the current figures instead of relying on an old chart.

For a buyer, the exemption does not transfer. A seller should expect the next bill, in the buyer's name, to be higher until the new owner files.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Towns County value?
sections.html:
File an appeal with the Board of Tax Assessors within 45 days of the date the assessment notice was mailed. The county site lists three grounds: taxability, value, and uniformity with similar properties. Complaints about the amount of tax levied are not part of an appeal.

If the assessors do not change the value, the appeal goes to the Board of Equalization, and then to Superior Court if you remain unhappy. Arbitration is available in place of the Board of Equalization. A family member can file for an owner who is away on military duty, within 90 days of the notice.

faqs.q: What is the Towns County property tax due date?
faqs.a: January 10 each year. The county tax site also lists April 1 for mobile homes. Mailed payments need a United States Postal Service postmark, not a metered one.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Towns County tax commissioner?
faqs.a: Call (706) 896-2267 or visit 48 River Street, Suite H, in Hiawassee. The office keeps weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and closes from noon to 1 p.m.

faqs.q: What penalties apply to late Towns County taxes?
faqs.a: Interest is added on the 10th of each month at prime plus 3% divided by 12. A 5% penalty is added after 120 days and every 120 days afterward, up to 20%. Mobile homes draw a 10% penalty on April 2.

faqs.q: How long do I have to challenge a Towns County assessment?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date the notice was mailed. File with the Board of Tax Assessors, which can be reached at (706) 896-3984, and the appeal then moves to the Board of Equalization if unresolved.

faqs.q: Does a Towns County homestead exemption pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. Once granted it renews each year for the same owner, but a change of ownership requires a new application. The buyer files with the tax assessor's office, and the deadline for the year is April 1.
